unsafe.text: A minute later Leo comes over the top of the dune, bent double, breathing hard.
He stands listening to the last of it, his hands on his knees.

unsafe.text: At the surgery door Dr Vosper stops, says goodnight to nobody in particular, and goes in.
Nobody moves. You think of a woman on the sand, talking to a boy. It's all right. You're a child.

review.old: I used to think that meant something.
review.new: I thought if we wrote things down carefully, we couldn't do much harm.

review.old: The pub thins out, but it doesn't empty. You stay where you are, your back to the wall, the clock over the bar in front of you.
review.new: The pub thins out but doesn't empty. You stay against the wall, facing the clock above the bar.

review.old: The road has gone.
review.new: The near stretch has gone under. Farther out, pale patches of road still show between the posts.

review.old: A quarter past nine. At the island end of the causeway, a pair of headlights flash twice and go out onto the road.
review.new: Thirteen minutes past nine. At the island end, headlights flash twice and move onto the causeway.

review.old: Assessor's eye. If a man goes out to sit out a big tide, the way he has for forty years — what does his house look like?
review.new: Assessor's eye. Tom has waited out big tides for forty years. If tonight were routine, what would his house look like?

review.old: You've seen his cabinet. Get in.
review.new: You've seen the cabinet. Tell Helen exactly what was there. Then I may need another pair of hands.

review.old: On the way down to the harbour he talks into his radio, short and flat: he is going out to the refuge box with a local boat.
review.new: On the way to the harbour, he radios in, clipped and flat: he is taking a local boat to the refuge box.

review.old: You kneel and touch Tom's hand. It's as cold as the iron ladder.
review.new: When Leo needs room, you move Tom's hand aside. It's as cold as the iron ladder.

review.old: We take him back. Nobody's dead till they're [[warm and dead]].
review.new: We take him back. The doctor decides. Get him out of this cold.

review.old: He doesn't say anything else.
review.new: Leo lowers the binoculars. He looks from the hut to the harbour.

review.old: Dr Vosper kneels on the wet stone and lifts each of Tom's eyelids with her thumb.
review.new: Dr Vosper checks Tom while Leo tells her what happened in the hut. Everyone else is made to stand back.

review.old: He's been gone an hour, Leo. I'm calling it.
review.new: He's gone, Leo. I'm recording the time.

review.old: Pinpoint. I can't be sure without bloods. But that's an [[opioid]]. And the cold did the rest.
review.new: Pinpoint. We need blood tests. An [[opioid]] is possible. The cold may have contributed.

review.old: Sweet. Whisky's not sweet.
review.new: Sweet. Like medicine.

review.old: Into his whisky. The bottle in his pocket is empty, and the flask is sweet and sticky. Tom drank his medicine without wanting to.
review.new: The whisky may contain his medicine. The empty bottle and sticky flask support that. They do not tell me who put it there.

review.old: Sweet. Whisky's not sweet. Whatever was in that bottle ended up in the flask.
review.new: An empty medicine bottle. A sticky flask. A possible connection, but I still need more.

review.old: Leo closes the door on him gently, the way you'd close it on someone sleeping. Then he turns the key and puts it in his pocket.
review.new: Leo closes the door gently, as if Tom were sleeping. He locks it and pockets the key.

review.old: You're a stranger. He asked you to his house at ten. You were alone in it. And you knew something was missing from his cabinet before anybod
review.new: He invited you for ten. A stranger, alone in his house. You knew something was missing from his cabinet before anyone else told me.

review.old: Probably he did it himself. Probably. But when CID get here, they'll ask me about you first. So I'd like to have an answer.
review.new: I don't know how he died. I do know you were in his house. Start with why.

review.old: Keys, please. I want you where I can see you.
review.new: Leave your keys with me, please. The road's underwater, and I need to know where you are.

review.old: The draft. If he searches you, he'll find it.
review.new: The draft. He is asking what you found, and you still haven't shown it.

review.old: You took that from a dead man's stove.
review.new: From the stove? Tell me exactly where it was.

review.old: At least I didn't have to find it.
review.new: Thank you for telling me. Next time, leave it where it is and call me.

review.old: And your pockets. All of them.
review.new: Anything else from the cottage? Empty your pockets, please.

review.old: He finds the half-burnt letter on the second pocket. He reads it twice, holding it by one corner.
review.new: You empty the second pocket last. The half-burnt letter lands between you. Leo reads it twice.

review.old: You took that from a dead man's stove.
review.new: From the stove? Tell me exactly where it was.

review.old: He bags it without another word. For the rest of the night, he doesn't use your name.
review.new: He bags it. The next question comes more slowly. He is checking every word now.

review.old: You stand at the door with your hand on the latch. Outside, the sea is loud. The road has been under it for an hour and a half.
review.new: Your hand rests on the latch. Outside, the sea roars. The causeway has been underwater for an hour and a half.

review.old: Through the wall, in the back room, a man you never got to speak to is lying under a pub blanket.
review.new: Beyond the wall, the man who never got to answer your question lies under a pub blanket.

review.old: Photo 4. The same car on the sand, after the tide. Somebody has taken a picture through the open door.
review.new: Photo 4. The car at low water, before recovery. Someone photographed the driver's seat through the open door.

review.old: Look again.
review.new: The recovery note fixes when the photograph was taken. Compare the driving position, not the water around the car.

review.old: There was never room for your feet behind her. You used to sit with your knees against the back of her seat and complain, and she never move
review.new: Behind her seat, you could stretch your legs. She needed it close to the pedals. She never drove with it pushed back.

review.old: You were at Tom's door at half six, Mr Marsh.
review.new: Did you see Tom before he came into the pub, Mr Marsh?

review.old: On his step. He never let me past the step.
review.new: Half past six. At his cottage. On the step, actually. He wouldn't let me inside.

review.old: I thought it was hello. I didn't stop.
review.new: I told myself he was signalling the boat. They'd seen each other. They didn't need me.

review.old: Dad checked.
review.new: My father's notes say that was checked. I've asked CID to check it again.

review.old: Nobody sits seven minutes on the phone with the sea coming in. Not about dinner. "Friday will finish me." I heard you say it to Tom at ten t
review.new: Seven minutes, with the sea coming in. Not about dinner. "Friday will finish me." That's what you told Tom at 19:50.

review.old: A [[bribe]] is a fine and a scandal. The other thing is the rest of your life. You understand why I'd rather you knew the first.
review.new: Yes, a [[bribe]]. You think I killed him. I'd rather you knew what I was actually doing.

review.old: First straight thing anyone's told me tonight.
review.new: Thank you. I'll record what he said. The call still needs checking.

review.old: Look again.
review.new: The clean bottle and full flask need explaining. Neither tells you who added anything, or when.

review.old: A man with shaking hands pours a bottle of syrup into a flask, in the wind, in the dark. Then he polishes the empty bottle, and puts it back
review.new: Suppose Tom added the medicine himself. He then cleaned the empty bottle, despite his shaking hands, and returned it to a sooty pocket.

review.old: Nobody does that.
review.new: Possible. But it leaves a lot unexplained.

review.old: And the flask. Fill it. Long night. Fergus filled it to the top at nine. A full flask has no room for a bottle of syrup.
review.new: Fergus filled the flask at nine. Tom could have emptied some later. The full flask alone proves nothing.

review.old: Whatever was in it was in the whisky before it was poured.
review.new: But somebody rinsed the TOM bottle while the boat was out. Why clean the source, if Tom only dosed his own flask?

review.old: He didn't touch that bottle. Not tonight.
review.new: The medicine could already have been in the whisky. The clean vial could have been planted.

review.old: Then it's not suicide.
review.new: Then we can't treat this as suicide.

review.old: Not suicide: clean syrup bottle in a sooty pocket; flask full at nine — the drug was in the TOM bottle before Fergus poured. Then someone ri
review.new: Working theory: the TOM whisky may have been tampered with before Fergus poured it. The rinsed bottle and clean vial need investigation and

review.old: You can go. Where I can see you.
review.new: Stay near the harbour. If you remember anything else, come straight back.

review.old: Leo's car was at the head of the road. I had my bag on the seat beside me. I thought, if he stops me and asks what's in it…
review.new: Leo was at the head of the causeway. My bag on the next seat. If he stopped me and asked what was inside…

review.old: Right. Thank you. That's the first time tonight anyone's told me before I had to ask.
review.new: All right. I'll record both things: what she brought, and what you saw still sealed.

review.old: The keeper's cottage is dark. When Leo opens the door, Skerry is lying in the hall. His nose is against the bottom of the back door, the doo
review.new: The hall lamp is still on. Leo opens the door. Skerry is lying on the rug.

review.old: The label under the dial is yellow with age. The number is written in the same hard, careful hand as every label in this house.
review.new: The label below the keypad has yellowed. The number is written in the same careful hand as every other label here.

review.old: “You were called today at twenty-one eleven hours. The caller [[withheld]] their number.”
review.new: “Your last call was received at twenty-one eleven hours. The caller [[withheld]] their number.”

review.old: The phone company can. That's [[paperwork]]. Days.
review.new: I've asked for the records. That's [[paperwork]]. They won't reach us before the tide turns.

review.old: Skerry doesn't lift his chin from the floor. Only his eyes follow you. He is still waiting for one particular step on the path.
review.new: Skerry follows you with his eyes. He stays on the rug, waiting for one particular step on the path.

review.old: You stayed on the slipway while they went out. This is the first time you see the inside of the box tonight.
review.new: Leo showed you these on the slipway. Now there is time to read the wall properly.

review.old: A man going out to die doesn't wave a lamp at the sea. He waves it at someone.
review.new: He kept signalling towards the boat. It looks as though he was trying to reach someone.

review.old: Look again. Dying men don't do the readings.
review.new: Look at the lamp. He was signalling towards the boat, not the shore.

review.old: A man going out to die doesn't wave a lamp at the sea. He waves it at someone.
review.new: He kept signalling towards the boat. It looks as though he was trying to reach someone.

review.old: Mobiles: Callum (harbour, getting the boat ready). Gideon (causeway — on a call?). Leo (head of the road). Dr Vosper (driving back to Tom's)
review.new: Mobiles: Callum, preparing his boat. Gideon, an incoming call on the mainland. Leo, at the road. Dr Vosper, near the pub.

review.old: That's how he knows who you are. You realise you've been waiting all night for someone to say her name to your face.
review.new: He says her name as if he knows what it costs you to hear it.

review.old: He stands up so fast the boat rocks under him. Skerry is on his feet too, very still.
review.new: He steps towards you so sharply the boat rocks under him. Skerry rises too, very still.

review.old: Tom's tide logbook. It falls open at a page it has fallen open at many times.
review.new: You fold back the plastic. Tom's tide logbook falls open at a page worn softer than the rest.

review.old: Twenty past one. Callum stands in the wheelhouse door with his arms folded. He hasn't sat down since you said the word 'hearing'.
review.new: Callum moves to the wheelhouse door and folds his arms. Twenty past one. Your threat still hangs between you.

review.old: You don't say anything. You have waited twenty years. You can wait a little longer.
review.new: You take one step back. His mouth keeps moving. For a moment, you cannot make the words join up.

review.old: You have never heard your mother's last words. You hear them now, in a fisherman's voice, twenty years late.
review.new: You have never heard what your mother said after the crash. Now a fisherman gives you those words, twenty years late.

review.old: I believed her. I wanted to.
review.new: I let her say it. That was easier than asking who she'd called.

review.old: He says it without bitterness, like the weather on a day long gone.
review.new: He says it carefully. Each word gives him somewhere to stop. He doesn't stop.

review.old: He takes out his phone again. Not for the photo this time. He thumbs to the call list and holds it out to you.
review.new: Callum takes out his phone and opens the call list. The screen lights his face. He holds it out to you.

review.old: I couldn't open it.
review.new: I couldn't make myself read it.

review.old: I couldn't open it.
review.new: I couldn't make myself read it.

review.old: Leo takes it. For a second he just holds it, like a baby someone has pushed into his arms.
review.new: Leo writes Callum's words down before he takes the book. Then he checks the wrapper and holds it under the lamp.

review.old: At half past eight the road was dry. 0.0. Someone made it flooded afterwards, in a different pen. And someone came for Tom at a quarter to n
review.new: At 20:30 the road was dry. Someone later changed that to 'flooded', using another pen. At 20:45, someone fetched Tom.

review.old: Find bones on that site and nothing gets built for a year.
review.new: If there's a grave under those footings, the rigs can't simply dig through it.

review.old: I thought you might.
review.new: All right. We stay together. Tell me if you need to stop.

review.old: Wooden [[survey pegs]] with orange tape, the kind they hammer in before the drilling starts. They have been pulled up and thrown aside in a
review.new: Wooden [[survey pegs]], orange tape: markers hammered in before drilling. Someone pulled them up and threw them aside in a heap.

review.old: Three pegs. Pulled tonight — the sand on their points is still damp.
review.new: Three uprooted pegs. Damp sand still clings to their points.

review.old: Dark, fresh sand. Someone has been digging here for a long time.
review.new: Dark sand, freshly disturbed. You cannot tell how long the digging took.

review.old: Leo doesn't stop him. Neither do you.
review.new: Leo catches Skerry's collar and draws him back. A pale curve already shows through the disturbed sand.

review.old: It doesn't take long. Whoever was here had already done most of the work.
review.new: Leo photographs the hollow before he touches anything. Whoever came before you has left the sand loose.

review.old: Leo digs on with his hands, wider, deeper. Nothing.
review.new: He sweeps the torch over the exposed hollow, keeping his feet outside its edge.

review.old: That's all of her that's here. Whoever it was took the rest.
review.new: Only this is exposed. The rest may have been moved. We need a proper search.

review.old: The dunes: only the skull was left. Whoever dug took the rest of her.
review.new: The dunes: a skull in a freshly disturbed hollow. No other remains visible. Someone drove away without lights.

review.old: Dr Vosper kneels beside the hollow before Leo can seal the bag. She doesn't touch what is inside. She turns it in the torchlight, slowly, wi
review.new: Dr Vosper kneels beside the hollow. She holds the bag by its edges and turns it towards the torch. She never touches the skull.

review.old: Ten past two. Leo is waiting for you at the estate gate below the big house. The estate's old Land Rover is standing in Gideon's yard, mud t
review.new: Ten past two. Leo is waiting at the estate gate below the big house.

review.old: He doesn't knock. Not alone, not with that bag in his hand.
review.new: He keeps the bag close. One officer, an unsecured house, and people he has to get back safely.

review.old: CID can knock.
review.new: We'll come back with CID. Nobody goes in there now.

review.old: Twenty years and more I've been a good doctor. Except for one morning.
review.new: I've told myself one morning didn't make me a bad doctor. It didn't make that morning go away.

review.old: It's the middle of the night. It can wait for the light.
review.new: I can't face what might be up there tonight. Go. I'll stay here.

review.old: Leo looks at you. Then he goes alone.
review.new: Leo goes down to the Mairi Rose. You wait under the harbour lamp while he talks to Callum.

review.old: An old cream telephone on a shelf behind the bar, its cord long enough to reach the cellar steps.
review.new: An old cream telephone sits on the shelf behind the bar. Its curled cord rests beside the receiver.

review.old: Nell pulls it without a word. Fergus lifts the glass an inch towards you, then towards the bottle on the shelf.
review.new: You call down for a half. Nell returns to pour it. Fergus raises the glass towards you, then towards Tom's bottle.

review.old: Nell pulls it without a word. Fergus lifts the glass an inch towards you, then towards the bottle on the shelf.
review.new: You call down for a half. Nell returns to pour it. Fergus raises the glass towards you, then towards Tom's bottle.

review.old: He taught me the road when I was a kid. Made me say it back to him, like a times table. Never walk it at the flood. If it catches you, climb
review.new: He taught me as a kid. Like learning my times tables. Never walk it at the flood. If it catches you, climb.

review.old: He taught me the road when I was a kid. Made me say it back to him, like a times table. Never walk it at the flood. If it catches you, climb
review.new: He taught me as a kid. Like learning my times tables. Never walk it at the flood. If it catches you, climb.

review.old: If it's about Tom Ashby, he's my patient and I can't discuss him. If it's about anything else, I'm late.
review.new: Then ask Tom what he wants to tell you. He's my patient. I won't discuss him on a doorstep.

review.old: If it's about Tom Ashby, he's my patient and I can't discuss him. If it's about anything else, I'm late.
review.new: Then ask Tom what he wants to tell you. He's my patient. I won't discuss him on a doorstep.

review.old: Whoever had that wasn't talking after it.
review.new: A serious blow. I wouldn't expect anyone to speak after that.

review.old: I wrote “fell from the harbour wall”. I didn't send him for an X-ray. I knew where the harbour wall was, and I knew where the causeway was.
review.new: I wrote “fell from the harbour wall”. No X-ray. I knew that wall. I knew the causeway too.
